name: SkyCity Entertainment Group Limited
overview: SkyCity Entertainment Group owns and operates regulated, monopoly-licensed casino and integrated entertainment precincts in Auckland, Hamilton and Queenstown (New Zealand) and Adelaide (South Australia), plus a small online casino serving New Zealand customers out of Malta. The business combines gaming (electronic gaming machines and table games) with hotels, food and beverage, conventions and entertainment, anchored by Auckland's Sky Tower and the newly opened New Zealand International Convention Centre (NZICC). Dual-listed on the NZX and ASX under 'SKC', it is currently working through a multi-year regulatory remediation and balance-sheet reset following AML/AUSTRAC penalties in Adelaide, a New Zealand host-responsibility licence suspension, and a ~37% dilutive equity raise completed in August 2025.

business_model.summary: Revenue is generated from four regulated casino precincts (gaming machines, table games, automated table games) plus non-gaming hospitality (hotels, food & beverage, conventions, car parking, Sky Tower attractions). Gaming is the dominant profit driver but is now subject to mandatory Carded Play in New Zealand, which management estimated depressed FY26 EBITDA by $20-30m. Non-gaming revenue (hotels, F&B, conventions, NZICC) is a growing but still minority contributor, expected to scale as the NZICC ramps through FY27-FY28. Revenue is largely transactional/discretionary (casino visitation and spend), not contracted or subscription-based, making it directly exposed to consumer discretionary spending and tourism cycles. Customer base is B2C (mass-market locals plus domestic/international tourists and a historically important, now much-reduced, international VIP/premium segment).

revenue_streams.name: SkyCity Auckland (flagship: casino, 3 hotels, NZICC, Sky Tower, F&B)
SkyCity Adelaide (Australia, sole SA casino licence)
Online casino (SkyCity Online Casino, NZ customers via Malta operator)
revenue_streams.trend: declining pre-regulation; strategic optionality for FY27/28 regulated licence

business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market gaming and hospitality customers, domestic and international tourists; historically included high-value international VIP play, now much smaller post-AML remediation
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~62% of FY26 group revenue (Auckland, Hamilton, Queenstown), Australia (Adelaide) ~38% in AUD, translated to NZD

main_competitors: The Star Entertainment Group (Australian casinos, under its own severe regulatory/financial distress)
Crown Resorts (Australian casinos, private under Blackstone)
Star Gold Coast / Treasury Brisbane and other Australian regional casinos
New Zealand hospitality, entertainment and hotel operators competing for discretionary spend
Emerging NZ-licensed online casino operators (post-2027 market opening) and offshore/illegal online gambling operators competing for the same wallet today
competitive_position.market_position: Sole legal casino operator in Auckland, Hamilton and Queenstown, and holder of South Australia's sole casino licence in Adelaide (exclusive rights to land-based casino gambling in SA to 2035, per the Approved Licensing Agreement). This is a structurally monopolistic position in each local market, not a market-share business in the conventional sense.

moat_factors.description: Sole casino licences in each of its four markets, expiring 2027 (Hamilton, renewal application submitted), 2040 (Queenstown, renewed Dec 2025), 2048 (Auckland) and 2035/2085 for Adelaide (exclusivity to 2035, licence itself to 2085). The moat is legally granted and therefore legally revocable or conditionable — the core tension in the investment case given the AUSTRAC and DIA/CBS enforcement history.
Sky Tower and the $750m NZICC in Auckland, plus large integrated precincts, are effectively impossible for a new entrant to replicate given exclusive licensing; high barrier to new supply.

moat_factors.factor: Brand / scale in each local market
moat_factors.description: Long-established, dominant local entertainment brand in each city it operates, though brand has been damaged by repeated AML and host-responsibility failures.

Large fixed cost base (precincts, staff, debt service) means EBITDA is highly sensitive to small revenue swings — the mechanism behind the EBITDA collapse from $338.7m (FY18) to $120.5m (FY26) on broadly flat revenue.

weaknesses: Licence conditions can be tightened or suspended by regulators (demonstrated: 5-day Auckland closure in 2024, Adelaide's ongoing enhanced-governance regime through at least January 2028)
Carded Play and other harm-minimisation mandates structurally depress gaming revenue with no clear offsetting growth lever yet proven
High operating leverage means margin, not revenue, is the swing factor — and margin has now compressed for a decade
Heavy net debt relative to a materially smaller earnings base post-impairments
Currency/geographic split (AUD Adelaide vs NZD reporting) adds translation risk on top of operating risk

growth_drivers: NZICC ramp: opened 11 February 2026, delivered 141 events and ~100,000 visitor days in its first ~5 months, with a confirmed FY27 pipeline of ~350,000 visits; management sees this driving incremental hotel, F&B and car park spend across the Auckland precinct, though the building itself is a large fixed cost, not a standalone profit centre

Regulated New Zealand online casino gambling market: enabling legislation passed and now in force; DIA estimates the market at NZ$1.36bn in annual gross gaming revenue; up to 15 licences to be auctioned, market opening pushed from December 2026 to June 2027 (FY28 the first full year); SkyCity has built a Malta-based team and new platform and intends to bid, but participation and share are both contingent on winning a licence at auction

Asset monetisation programme: original ~NZ$200m target by February 2027 now expected to be exceeded, with $74.5m unconditional sale of 99 Albert Street and Victoria Street properties (proceeds due September 2026) and a non-binding Heads of Agreement to sell the Grand Hotel Auckland; aggregate proceeds now guided at $275-300m, applied to debt paydown to take net debt/underlying EBITDA from 3.1x to below 2.0x in FY27
Cost-out programme: exceeded FY26 $10m target; expanded to $30m annualised benefits targeted in FY27, growing to $70m in FY28, supported by an external consultant-led organisational reset

Adelaide resolution: non-binding Heads of Agreement with the SA Commissioner (A$21m fine plus enhanced governance) is intended to draw a line under the CBS enforcement action, after which management plans a strategic review of the Adelaide business's long-term operating model
Potential dividend resumption once capital management objectives (investment-grade rating, net debt/EBITDA below 2.0x) are met — a re-rating catalyst if achieved

business.risk: Structural gaming revenue reset from Carded Play
business.description: Mandatory carded, account-based play across NZ casinos reduced FY26 EBITDA by an estimated $20-30m versus a non-carded base; management frames this as a one-off step-down already in the base, but it is unproven whether spend recovers or the base is now permanently lower

FY26 letter cites a recessionary environment, high fuel costs and interest rates pressuring consumer spending, particularly evident in Auckland and Adelaide; casino/entertainment spend is highly discretionary

Post-settlement, Adelaide is under review for its long-term operating model; the B3 remediation programme carries its own ongoing cost burden and a change of governance structure (majority independent non-executive directors by January 2028)
The $750m building is early in its ramp; converting event visitation into precinct spend (hotels, F&B, car parking) is management's stated challenge, not yet proven at scale over a full year

financial.risk: High leverage against a smaller earnings base
financial.description: Total debt of $719.3m against FY26 EBITDA of $120.5m (or $181.6m underlying) implies gearing well above historical norms; reported net debt/underlying EBITDA was 3.1x at FY26 year-end, guided to fall below 2.0x in FY27 contingent on successful, timely completion of asset sales

The Auckland car park concession sale process did not attract offers meeting the company's commercial objectives, illustrating that not every planned disposal completes on time or at expected value; remaining monetisation (Grand Hotel, other assets) is non-binding or in progress

S&P has SkyCity at BBB- with a history of negative-outlook commentary; management explicitly frames capital allocation (including any online licence bid) as subordinate to maintaining investment-grade metrics and covenant headroom (historical net debt/EBITDA covenant near 3.75x)

financial.risk: Dilution already realised, further dilution possible
financial.description: The August 2025 capital raise (NZ$240m at 70 cents/share, ~30% discount) took weighted average shares from 759m to 1,037m in FY26 and total shares on issue to over 1.1bn by August 2026; per-share metrics before FY26 are not comparable to after
Adelaide revenue and earnings are reported in AUD and translated into NZD group results, adding a currency layer on top of operating performance

regulatory.description: The Federal Court ordered SkyCity Adelaide to pay an AU$67m penalty in June 2024 for systemic AML/CTF non-compliance; this sits alongside, and is distinct from, the separate South Australian state regulatory action

Following the independent Brian Martin review (August 2025, which found SkyCity Adelaide and the Group suitable to hold/be associated with the licence, while noting past and ongoing issues), a non-binding Heads of Agreement was reached in June 2026 with the Commissioner for Liquor and Gambling: an A$21m fine plus enhanced governance (majority independent non-executive directors by January 2028), curbed CEO decision-making authority, 5-business-day breach reporting, an independent compliance auditor, and phase-out of cash transactions over A$4,999. This is materially better than licence loss but represents a long remediation tail with real operating constraints; the agreement is still non-binding pending ratification

regulatory.risk: New Zealand DIA / host responsibility enforcement
regulatory.description: DIA suspended SkyCity Auckland's casino operator licence for host-responsibility failures (a vulnerable customer allowed to lose over $1m across 23+ prolonged sessions between 2017-2021), resulting in a 5-day Auckland casino closure (September 2024, ~$5m EBITDA impact) — evidence that NZ's regulator will and has acted; Carded Play was SkyCity's principal remediation response but further DIA scrutiny of host responsibility remains an ongoing risk

Hamilton's licence (current term to 2027) is under renewal application for a further 15 years; Auckland (to 2048), Queenstown (renewed Dec 2025, to 2040) and Adelaide (exclusivity to 2035, licence to 2085) are secure for now, but each renewal is a discrete regulatory event, not a formality, given the recent compliance history

SkyCity's entry into the regulated NZ online casino market (DIA-estimated $1.36bn GGR market) depends on winning one of up to 15 licences at competitive auction; there is no guarantee of success, and any winning bid consumes capital that competes with debt reduction and dividend resumption

regulatory.risk: Problem gambling levies and harm-minimisation cost trend
regulatory.description: $4.3m paid in problem gambling levies in FY26 alone; the regulatory direction of travel in both NZ and Australia is toward more restrictive, not less restrictive, gaming settings

macro.description: Net interest expense was $27.5m in FY26 against $719.3m of debt; elevated rates directly compress an already thin pre-tax result (FY26 pre-tax loss of $12.1m before the tax benefit)

Queenstown and, to a lesser extent, Auckland and Adelaide, are exposed to international tourism flows and broader consumer cycles; management explicitly cited the Middle East conflict, fuel costs and interest rates as FY26 headwinds

The NZICC was delivered within its $750m cost envelope, reducing forward capex-cycle risk, though ongoing precinct capex and digital/technology investment remain a call on already-stretched free cash flow

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Australasian land-based casino gaming faces structural headwinds from tightening harm-minimisation regulation (carded/cashless play mandates), while integrated-resort/convention and online gaming are the industry's principal growth vectors. New Zealand's online casino market is a genuine new legal market opening in 2027, a rare structural growth opportunity in an otherwise mature/declining land-based segment.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately-to-highly cyclical: discretionary consumer and tourism spending, high operating leverage against a large fixed cost base means earnings swings are amplified relative to revenue swings
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-high given $719.3m of debt and negative-to-thin pre-tax profitability; each ratings/covenant metric is directly linked to the interest burden
key_input_costs: Labour (largest single opex line across ~4,700 employees)

recent_developments.event: SkyCity disclosed it received and rejected two confidential, unsolicited, non-binding takeover proposals in May 2026 — from a special situations fund managed by Oaktree Capital Management at an indicative NZ$0.70/share, and from an unnamed second party at an implied NZ$0.75/share. The Board judged both proposals inadequate and their conditions (8+ weeks due diligence, financing conditionality) problematic; neither party returned an improved offer.

FY2026 annual results released: reported revenue $878.9m (+6.5%), reported EBITDA $120.5m (-44.2%), reported NPAT $18.2m (-37.6%, aided by a $30.3m tax benefit against a pre-tax loss of $12.1m); underlying EBITDA $181.6m (-22.3%), in line with revised May 2026 guidance of $180-190m. Shares rose modestly (~4%) on the day, reflecting relief that guidance was met and progress on asset sales/cost-out, though the stock remains near the low end of its 52-week range.

Non-binding Heads of Agreement announced for the sale of the Grand Hotel in Auckland; unconditional sale of 99 Albert Street and Victoria Street properties for $74.5m (settlement due September 2026), taking aggregate expected monetisation proceeds guided at $275-300m, ahead of the original ~$200m target.

Non-binding Heads of Agreement with South Australia's Commissioner for Liquor and Gambling to resolve the CBS enforcement action stemming from the Brian Martin independent review: A$21m fine, enhanced governance and compliance commitments (majority independent NEDs by January 2028, curbed CEO authority, breach reporting, independent compliance auditor, phase-out of large cash transactions).

NZICC (New Zealand International Convention Centre) officially opened after achieving Practical Completion on 3 November 2025, within its $750m cost envelope; delivered via a public/stakeholder programme culminating in an inaugural Six60 concert.
Queenstown casino venue licence renewed, extending to 2040.

SkyCity completed a deeply discounted NZ$240m equity raise (placement + entitlement offer at 70 cents/share, a ~30% discount) to fund debt reduction and capital management objectives; total shares outstanding rose from ~759m to over 1.0bn, later exceeding 1.1bn.

Independent review by the Hon Brian Martin AO KC found SkyCity Adelaide suitable to continue holding the SA casino licence and the Group suitable to be a close associate, while identifying past and ongoing compliance issues — the foundation for the subsequent CBS settlement.

items.target: no explicit FY27 EBITDA range disclosed in the annual report excerpt reviewed; FY26 underlying EBITDA of $181.6m was delivered within the revised (May 2026) $180-190m guidance range
items.notes: Original FY26 guidance was revised down in May 2026; the $180-190m range was met

items.target: $30m annualised benefits in FY27, growing to $70m total annualised benefits by FY28
items.notes: FY26's original $10m target was exceeded; programme has been broadened beyond simple cost control to an operating-model reset focused on operating cash flow

Down from 3.1x at FY26 year-end; contingent on completing the $275-300m asset monetisation programme, with proceeds applied to debt reduction; explicitly stated to be achieved before any payment for an online casino licence

Comprises the unconditional $74.5m 99 Albert Street/Victoria Street sale (proceeds due September 2026) plus the non-binding Grand Hotel Auckland sale and other assets; the Auckland car park concession process has not yet produced an acceptable offer
Explicit precondition for any online casino licence spend and for dividend resumption

items.target: No dividend paid FY25 or FY26; company states it expects to be able to consider resuming dividends subject to achieving capital management objectives
items.period: not yet specified — contingent, likely FY2027 or later
items.notes: Explicitly conditional on net debt/EBITDA reduction and investment-grade rating maintenance

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jason Walbridge and Chair Julian Cook framed FY26 as 'a year of reset,' citing Carded Play, the NZICC opening and a significant cost-reduction programme as the major operational changes delivered under a difficult consumer and regulatory backdrop. FY27 priorities are explicitly stated as: complete the announced asset sales and reset the balance sheet; deliver $30m of annualised cost benefits (on track for $70m by FY28); finalise the Adelaide (CBS) regulatory agreement; advance the B3 Adelaide remediation programme; commence a strategic review of Adelaide's long-term operating model; and secure a New Zealand online casino licence with a 'disciplined approach to entry,' subordinate to maintaining investment-grade credit metrics.

bull_case: Two unsolicited takeover approaches at NZ$0.70 and NZ$0.75/share (versus a stock trading around NZ$0.51-0.60) suggest sophisticated financial buyers see embedded value in the licence portfolio and real estate that the market is not currently pricing — and signals the regulatory/balance-sheet overhang may be closer to a floor than an open-ended decline

Asset monetisation is ahead of plan (guided at $275-300m versus an original ~$200m target, with $74.5m already unconditionally sold), and successful execution could take net debt/underlying EBITDA below 2.0x in FY27, materially de-risking the balance sheet and reopening the path to dividend resumption

The NZICC and NZ online casino licensing represent genuine, non-trivial new revenue opportunities layered on top of an otherwise mature, monopoly-licensed core business — a rare structural growth vector for a casino operator, even if both are unproven at scale

The regulatory overhang in Adelaide has moved from open-ended enforcement risk (a licence-suitability review) to a defined, quantified settlement (A$21m fine plus governance conditions), reducing tail risk even if compliance costs remain elevated

Monopoly casino licences across four separate markets, with terms extending out to 2035-2085, still represent a structurally protected earnings base once cost-out benefits and Carded Play normalisation are annualised
bear_case: Earnings power has structurally roughly halved while the share count grew ~37% in FY26 alone (759m to 1,037m weighted average, now over 1.1bn shares outstanding): EBITDA fell from $338.7m in FY18 to $120.5m in FY26 on essentially flat revenue ($994.6m to $813.7m), and FY26 pre-tax result was a loss of $12.1m — the reported NPAT of $18.2m exists only because of a $30.3m tax benefit, not because the underlying business made money

Carded Play, tighter host-responsibility enforcement and the broader NZ/Australia regulatory direction of travel look like a permanent reset of the gaming revenue base, not a one-off dip — management's own $20-30m EBITDA impact estimate for FY26 alone illustrates the scale, and there is no proven mechanism by which that revenue returns

The regulatory record is one of repeated, serious failures, not a single event: an AU$67m Federal Court AML penalty, a further A$21m South Australian fine with governance conditions running to at least January 2028, and a 2024 5-day forced closure of the Auckland casino for host-responsibility failures — a company whose core competitive asset (its casino licences) has been directly and repeatedly put at risk by its own conduct

The asset monetisation programme is not fully de-risked: the Auckland car park concession process failed to attract an acceptable offer, illustrating that not every planned sale completes on time or at expected value, and a meaningful share of the $275-300m target remains non-binding (Grand Hotel Heads of Agreement) rather than contracted

Debt remains high ($719.3m) against a much smaller earnings base, with dividends suspended and resumption explicitly conditional on metrics not yet met; the board's own decision to reject two takeover approaches at 20-45% premiums to the pre-announcement price leaves shareholders dependent on management successfully executing a multi-year turnaround (cost-out, asset sales, Adelaide resolution, NZICC ramp, online licence) rather than crystallising value today
